title: Custom authentication handlers and API keys
hook: Not every caller uses JWT. Partner webhooks, internal jobs, and legacy integrations often send API keys or custom headers. AuthenticationHandler<TOptions> lets you plug those schemes into the same pipeline as Bearer tokens.

blocks.text: ASP.NET Core authentication is extensible via AuthenticationHandler<TOptions>. Each scheme (JwtBearer, Cookies, ApiKey) reads credentials from the request, validates them, and returns AuthenticateResult.Success with a ClaimsPrincipal or Fail. API key patterns hash keys at rest, scope keys to tenants, rotate on leak, and never log raw keys. You can register multiple schemes and use [Authorize(AuthenticationSchemes = "ApiKey,Bearer")] for endpoints accepting either.

entries.plainDefinition: HandlesAuthenticateAsync reads credentials; HandleChallengeAsync produces 401 response.
Named authentication mechanism registered with AddAuthentication().AddScheme<>.
Long-lived secret sent in header or query — identifies a client app, not a human user.
Store SHA-256 or bcrypt hash of key; compare hash on request — plaintext key shown once at creation.
entries.example: Similar to password hashing — never store ak_live in database plaintext

blocks.text: Machine-to-machine integrations often predate OAuth at the partner. A well-designed API key handler integrates with policies, logging, and rate limiting. Poor patterns — query string keys in URLs, shared master keys, keys in git — appear in OWASP API Top 10. Senior engineers explain when API keys beat OAuth client credentials (simplicity, webhook callbacks) and when they do not (user delegation, fine-grained consent).

blocks.title: Keys are secrets
blocks.body: Transmit API keys in headers (X-Api-Key or Authorization: ApiKey ...), not query strings — URLs land in logs, browser history, and referrer headers.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: HandleAuthenticateAsync
items.body: Read header, lookup hash in database/cache, build ClaimsPrincipal with client id and scopes.

items.title: Success or NoResult
items.body: NoResult lets other schemes try; Fail stops with authentication failure.

items.title: Authorization
items.body: Same policy pipeline — RequireClaim for key scopes or separate policy for machine clients.

diagram.title: Multiple authentication schemes
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  REQ[Request] --> AUTHN[UseAuthentication]
  AUTHN --> JWT[JwtBearerHandler]
  AUTHN --> APIKEY[ApiKeyHandler]
  JWT -->|Success| USER[ClaimsPrincipal]
  APIKEY -->|Success| USER
  JWT -->|NoResult| APIKEY
  USER --> AUTHZ[Authorization policies]

snippet.label: ApiKeyHandler skeleton
snippet.explanation: NoResult when header absent allows JWT scheme on multi-scheme endpoints. Fail when header present but invalid — distinct from missing credentials on single-scheme routes.

snippet.label: Register scheme and dual-auth endpoint
snippet.explanation: Comma-separated schemes accept first successful handler. Webhook-only routes restrict to ApiKey scheme so Bearer tokens cannot impersonate webhook identity.

snippet.label: Hashed key validation service
snippet.explanation: Prefix narrows DB lookup; bcrypt verifies without storing plaintext. Rotate by deactivating row and issuing new key.

snippet.label: Rate limit and audit API key usage
snippet.explanation: Production API keys need per-client rate limits and audit trails keyed by client_id — proves abuse investigation without logging secrets.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Single global API key in appsettings committed to git. Keys in query strings. Logging full key on failed auth. No rotation or scope per key. Using Fail instead of NoResult on multi-scheme endpoints when header is absent.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: metrics on ApiKey validation failures by prefix (brute force detection). Alert when one client_id exceeds rate limit. Compare API key traffic vs OAuth client_credentials — migrate partners to OAuth when they need scoped consent and rotation automation. HMAC request signing (AWS SigV4 style) is stronger than static keys for high-value webhooks — custom handler validates signature + timestamp skew.

blocks.title: API key vs OAuth client credentials
What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Storing plaintext API keys in SQL. Saying custom handlers bypass authorization middleware. Not knowing difference between NoResult and Fail. Recommending query parameter API keys for convenience.

interviewTakeaways: AuthenticationHandler<TOptions> plugs custom schemes (API keys, HMAC) into UseAuthentication.
Hash keys at rest; header-only transport; prefix + bcrypt verify; show plaintext once at creation.
Production tip: per-client_id rate limits; audit logs without raw keys; rotate on leak.
60s: Implement HandleAuthenticateAsync — read header, validate hash, return ClaimsPrincipal. Register AddScheme. Use AuthenticationSchemes on policies. NoResult lets JWT try next.
Follow-up: when would HMAC-signed requests beat static API keys?
commonPitfalls: Saying 'API keys replace OAuth always' gets you rejected — keys suit M2M simplicity; OAuth gives standard scopes and rotation.
Plaintext keys in database — store bcrypt hash only; treat leak like password breach.
Strong answer: 'Custom handler integrates with same policy pipeline. Keys scoped per client, hashed, rate-limited. Webhooks use dedicated scheme policy.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: Header check middleware equals HandleAuthenticateAsync — ASP.NET advantage is unified [Authorize] and multiple schemes.
Passport custom Strategy validate callback mirrors ApiKeyHandler building user object from key lookup.
